As the line in the song Big Yellow Taxi goes "Don't it always seem to go, that you don't know what you've got 'til it's gone." Texas is about to find out just how true that is.

Because Texas just ran an experiment that nobody designed, and the results should raise the eyebrows of anyone who cares about grid reliability, no matter where you live.

For the last four years, Bitcoin miners have been the most flexible large load on the ERCOT grid. When temperatures hit record highs in August 2023, Riot Platforms and others curtailed their power usage by more than 95% during peak demand, stabilizing the grid as they did so. ERCOT didn’t have to ask twice. The miners powered down in seconds, and stayed off for over 120 hours throughout August, often ramping up and down consumption to the precise level needed by ERCOT for grid stability in extreme conditions. There were no blackouts, and no emergency, just Bitcoin mining doing what only Bitcoin mining can do.

That wasn’t an anomaly. During 2022’s winter storms, Texas-based miners curtailed power consumption by 98-99%. In ERCOT’s classification, Bitcoin miners are Controllable Load Resources. They can cycle consumption on and off in less than a minute and ramp from zero to hundreds of megawatts over very short timeframes.

This matters because during these same four years, Texas renewables expanded significantly. Solar alone nearly quadrupled, going from about 4% in 2021 to ~12.8% in 2025.

More renewables means more intermittency. More intermittency means the grid needs more flexible demand. Bitcoin miners filled that role. When the wind blew and the sun shone, they absorbed surplus energy. When the grid got tight, they powered down. The network kept running and the lights stayed on…

Now they’re leaving. Here’s what that means for Texas, and for how the world views Bitcoin mining.

What 226 Gigawatts Looks Like

ERCOT’s large-load interconnection queue jumped from 63 GW at the end of 2024 to 226 GW in 2025. To give an idea how big this queue is, that means there is three times the entire grid's current peak capacity wanting to consume power on the grid. The queue has nearly quadrupled in a single year. Unsurprisingly, AI companies account for roughly 73% of those new applications.

But here’s the problem for the grid - at the same time, Bitcoin mining companies themselves are converting into AI companies. Core Scientific signed a $10 billion hosting deal with CoreWeave. IREN secured a $9.7 billion, five-year deal with Microsoft. Hut 8 landed a $7 billion Google-backed lease. Riot Platforms sits on 1.7 GW of land and power permits that hyperscalers desperately need to bypass the 5-7 year wait for new utility substations. Galaxy Digital secured $460 million to convert its Texas mining site into an AI data center with a 15-year CoreWeave lease.

From a shareholder perspective, the logic is obvious. AI hosting contracts generate 80-90% operating margins. But from a grid perspective, the trade is something else entirely.

The Distinction That Changes Everything

Bitcoin mining is interruptible. AI inference and training runs are not.

A Bitcoin miner can power down in under a minute and lose nothing except the sats it would have mined during those minutes. That’s a calculable, recoverable cost. An AI training run that gets interrupted mid-computation can lose days of work. The workload cannot pause. The power cannot fluctuate.

ERCOT CEO Pablo Vegas has projected that grid needs will grow from approximately 85 GW to 150 GW within six years. OpenAI and Oracle’s Stargate complex in Abilene alone will require 1.2 GW when completed.

So the grid is simultaneously losing its most flexible large load and gaining its most inflexible one. Read that last sentence again. If you thought “that doesn’t sound good for grid stability” you’re absolutely right.

The thing that made Bitcoin miners valuable to ERCOT during every winter storm and summer heatwave since 2021 - their willingness to power down when asked - is precisely what AI operations cannot do.

Grid operators don’t hold press conferences to say “Hey everyone, we’re worried.” Their job is to preserve the belief of everyone that electricity is always available at the flick of a switch. But when ERCOT reorganises its entire large-load interconnection process, contracts McKinsey, and rewrites its rules for how flexible demand connects to the grid - all within months of Bitcoin miners heading for the exit - their actions are saying the quiet part about their level of concern out loud.

That’s a retrospective performance review of Bitcoin mining’s grid contribution.

The rules aren’t finalised yet. They won’t be until later in 2026.

The Irony

Let’s name what’s happening plainly.

For four years, Bitcoin miners were falsely labeled “parasites”, “energy hogs”, and “a threat to reliability” on the Texas grid, and other grids. Yet during that entire period, they were the grid’s most cooperative large load, powering down voluntarily during every major stress event, earning demand response revenues for doing exactly what the grid needed them to do.

Now those same companies are converting to AI. The financial press is celebrating it as a smart business pivot. But the bigger question no one in the media is asking is: what replaces the flexible load?

Renewable energy penetration in Texas has increased substantially during the period of significant Bitcoin mining presence. Wind and solar combined went from roughly 28% of ERCOT generation in 2021 to over 36% in the first nine months of 2025. According to former ERCOT grid operator Brad Jones, that expansion was enabled, in part, by having 3 GW of flexible Bitcoin mining demand that could absorb surplus renewable energy when it was abundant and release it when the grid needed it.

The irony: the very load type that enabled higher renewable penetration is being replaced by a load type that will make higher renewable penetration extremely difficult to manage. As Rhodes et al said in their 2021 study, grids that use a lot of Bitcoin mining can allow more VRE (solar and wind) onto their grid, whereas grids that have more AI datacenters need more fossil fuel based generation. To put it in crude, simplistic terms: flexible consumers enable more inflexible generation (solar and wind), but inflexible consumers require more flexible generation (coal and gas).

Where This Goes Next

There’s a speculative angle here worth naming, because some companies are already building toward it.

Marathon Digital (MARA) has been developing what they call a “Digital Energy” model. The idea: facilities that run AI as the primary workload but dedicate a portion of their power capacity (~3%) to Bitcoin mining. The mining serves as the flexible buffer. When the grid needs power, the mining pauses. The AI keeps running. The facility remains a controllable load resource without sacrificing its primary revenue stream.

They’re deploying modular racks in their Granbury, Texas facility that can dynamically switch workloads between mining and AI compute based on real-time grid conditions.

If this works, the conclusion is striking: AI data centers will need Bitcoin mining in order to be good grid citizens. A small allocation of hashrate as the cost of grid compliance.

In other words, Bitcoin mining would have a second-coming as the load balancer that every AI datacenter needs in order to be a good citizen on the grid.

I don’t know yet whether MARA’s technology works at scale. The load-balancing challenge is real. But the direction is clear: if ERCOT is going to absorb 150 GW of demand within six years, and most of that demand is inflexible AI, then something needs to provide the flexibility that Bitcoin miners used to provide. And the most efficient solution might be … Bitcoin mining itself.

The Back-Validation

What the ERCOT data tells us, read in context, is that Bitcoin mining was never a grid problem. It was a grid solution that nobody wanted to credit. That’s why the moment it started leaving, the grid operator has had to hire a large team of consultants to try to figure out what to do next.

Texas’ looming struggle in the wake of a Bitcoin mining exodus, while negative for Texas, is very bullish for the future of Bitcoin mining, and therefore how the world views Bitcoin, because it is a real-life at-scale Split test of what happens to grids with and without the world’s most flexible load.

Sometimes you don’t know what you had until you’ve replaced it with something that can’t do the same job.

What if Bitcoin revolutionizes energy as much as it does money?

What if the impact of Bitcoin’s energy revolution was as positive to humanity as the impact of Bitcoin’s monetary revolution?

What if right under our noses Bitcoin’s impact on energy was already as big as Bitcoin’s impact on money?

When Satoshi created Bitcoin, he birthed not just a monetary revolution, but the twin revolutionary forces of a new approach to money and a new approach to energy.

While Bitcoin’s monetary revolution was by design, the energy revolution is by accident. For this reason, it often doesn’t get the same coverage and attention.

This accidental Bitcoin revolution is already showing signs of reshaping humanity in a way that has the potential to impact all of our lives.

In this article, I cover the five reasons why convergence between energy and Bitcoin mining is happening at pace.

Let’s get started:

As Lyn Alden points out, money is fundamentally broken. It turns out that energy is fundamentally broken too. Lyn Alden wrote a book on the first point.

First, some context on energy and grids:

Unlike the Internet, Energy needs wires to transport. Lots of them.

Unlike a digital nomad using the Internet to live freely anywhere in the world, energy is a prisoner of time and space.

Energy cannot be effectively stored at scale (even with batteries) for more than four hours.

Energy cannot be efficiently transported either. Grid operators say transmission incurs around a “7% loss”, but like inflation, the real figure is much higher than the official figure.

Energy-generation also cannot be effectively coupled with the energy-use at the right time of day, leading to massive peaks and troughs in energy demand.

When old, centrally architected grids meet aggressive decarbonization and energy scaleup goals, we see five ways in which the systems we use to distribute Energy are broken. Yes, Bitcoin fixes this, it’s already started fixing this, and it is happening at pace. Here’s how.


1. Centralized

Like financial systems, today's energy transmission and distribution systems are highly centralized. Grids are like the energy equivalent of a central bank: they are inefficient at getting resources to people who need it equitably. Micro-grids are the solution, but the challenge has historically been that with a smaller population being serviced, the statistical chance of power getting generated at a time people don’t need it is even higher.

How Bitcoin accelerates development of decentralized energy systems

Bitcoin solves this problem, because when people don’t need power, you simply mine Bitcoin. That pays off the micro-grid faster while lowering the cost of power to micro-grid users.

This beneficial impact is not theory, it is exactly what Gridless has already shown is possible in four African villages, taking over 8000 people out of energy poverty already.

Having proven this works in theory and in practice, there is now no barrier to scaling the renewable-microgrid/Bitcoin mining hybrid solution throughout Africa. Ultimately this isn’t just a solution for Africa, decentralization could in decades to come be the global way that energy is delivered. It would be both possible and poetic that a decentralized monetary system were the catalyst for the decentralization of energy systems.

2. Subsidized

Solar is a cool technology. What's more intuitively appealing than capturing the abundant energy of the sun! It's efficient, renewable, zero marginal cost power.

But have government subsidies for solar worked? There's a litany of examples of where Government solar subsidies have led to heavily under-capacity, unwanted, untransportable, or even obsolescent solar farms. This has happened across the world, and includes EU, Northern Territory Australia, Spain, Texas, China, India, South Africa, Chile and Finland, where aside from the wasted energy, a total of 2750 GW of renewable energy is stuck in interconnection queues in these 10 regions alone.

How Bitcoin offers governments a subsidy-free future, while fixing the problems that existing subsidies created


Bitcoin mining fixes each case mentioned above. It does this by buying up wasted/ stranded solar energy that got overbuilt in the wrong places due to government subsidies. Bitcoin mining also helps politicians by making short-sighted political decisions around subsidies look smart after the fact.

Nowhere is this more apparent than in Texas.

Texas got solar subsidies through Federal tax credits (e.g: Roserock Solar Farm, 328 MW).

Before Bitcoin mining came onto Texas’ ERCOT grid, solar and wind farms were under-utilized due to

1. Grid Constraints: Congestion in W.Texas limits solar export to cities like Dallas

2. Curtailment: Solar farms in the Permian Basin compete with wind and fossil fuels, leading to wasted energy during low-price periods

3. Market Volatility: Subsidies encouraged overbuilding, but falling power prices reduce profitability

Because of this underutilization, pressure mounted to stop producing more wasteful solar (and wind farms). But in 2021, Bitcoin mining companies entered onto the grid and started buying the solar and wind energy that no-one else wanted. Sometimes they co-located on the solar or wind farm. At other times they provided a buyer for that otherwise wasted renewable energy. Then they helped counterbalance their intermittency once on the grid. These three factors resulted in solar and wind farm generators being able to lift their generation capacity from 80 GW in 2021 to 130 GW in late 2024.

Meanwhile, a peer-reviewed study in Heliyon provided further evidence that it was likely Bitcoin mining that was causing the difference, showing that a 50MW solar farm would normally take 8.1 years to become profitable, but using Bitcoin mining it could reduce this to a mere 3.5 year payback. Like all responsible business owners, the solar generator would use profits to expand their operation.

3. Politicized

Today, what does the political left care more about?

  • environmental security (and to an extent energy equity)

What does the political right care more about?

  • energy security

It didn’t use to be this way. In the 1980s, Conservative Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher spoke actively about climate change and stated the UK must move beyond coal. By contrast, on the political left, prominent figures in the British Labour Party including both leader Neil Kinnock and former leader Michael Foot argued that coal was a vital source of jobs, vital to the economy, and vital to UK’s energy security following the 1973 oil crisis.

So while these alignments are tribal, which tribe aligns with which set of arguments can and has changed radically over time.

I recently wrote about how the decarbonization policies of today’s left and the energy security policies of today’s right have been implemented in a foolish way.

Until we look for solutions that combine the best of what the left and right want, we will continue to yo-yo from the decarbonization goals of the the left to the energy security goals of the right, while ultimately both fail to adequately deliver either goal.

How Bitcoin is a non-partisan tool for decarbonization and energy security


Without a tool, the paragraph above that you just read is just ideological hope. Bitcoin is the tool that turns the statement from ideological hope to implementable reality.

Bitcoin increases energy security by making local sources of power generation more profitable. But Bitcoin also allows us to profitably decarbonize at the same time, in ways which include:

  • accelerating the renewable energy transition (Lal et al, 2023)
  • obviating the need for carbon-intensive gas peaker plants (Bruno et al, 2023)
  • stabilizing the grid while it scales to handle more renewables (Rudd et al, 2023)
  • halving the payback time for solar farms (Hakimi et al, 2024)
  • accelerating renewable microgrid development (Moghimi et al 2024)
  • reducing methane emissions from landfills (Sechrest et al, 2024)

These are not ideal theoretical possibilities, these benefits exist right now. I've documented the numerous case studies where they’re occurring in this longer article.

4. Fossilized

By fossilized, I don’t mean fossil-fuel based grids, I mean grids that are really old.

How bad is the situation? Well, imagine there’s no wireless cell phone network and all communication must be done over a wired landline phone network that hasn’t been maintained or upgraded for 30 years: that’s our modern energy infrastructure. It’s fossilized, under-maintained and in no position to handle additional load, or additional variable renewable energy (VRE) generation

That’s the state of grids throughout the world (here’s the top 10 examples of badly aging grids.

But does this have an impact: The short answer is “yes”, it fundamentally impacts how much new VRE can be placed on them, a phenomenon that has been widely covered in mainstream media.

Many grids are struggling to meet today’s capacity, let alone the future much harder demands placed upon grids by the more constant load-balanced needed when you have high concentrations of VRE – aka Solar and Wind – on them.

How Bitcoin proves an almost cost-neutral fix to the issue of aging grids

Bitcoin mining has been shown to largely, if not completely, remedy the issue (Norris et al, 2025) of load balancing new VRE, avoiding the expensive grid-upgrade costs that would otherwise be incurred in order to handle more intermittency. In short, Bitcoin mining is a hack that means you can put more VRE onto even an aging grid, without astronomical upgrade costs. In fact, it’s the only way you can put more VRE onto an aging grid without astronomical upgrade costs.

5. Wasteful

On the grid, wasted energy is normally renewable energy: either its solar or wind produced at a time of day when people don’t want it, or a part of the country where people aren’t around to use it. Then there is hydro which in the rainy season of many nations including Norway, New Zealand, China, Costa Rica, simply flows over the top of the dam on a seasonal basis.

While batteries and pumped hydro are part of the solution, they are not the whole solution. Batteries will only store for 4 hours (not much use if you have surplus wind during a storm for 96 hours), and due to topographical issues, pumped-hydro is only a solution for a small subset of hydro-dams.

What this means is, without a flexible user of energy, all this renewable power will continue to be squandered. For example in the UK, Scottish Wind farms now waste 20% of their energy.

What is the cost of this? Enormous. One site, Wastedwind.energy quantifies how much wind energy alone the UK wastes on a daily basis. Just 78 days into 2025: $417 Million of wasted power.

How Bitcoin prevents the wasting of renewable energy

Pavel Grachev calculates that while Bitcoin could not have stopped the expense of needing to fire up gas plants, had wind farms been used for Bitcoin mining rather than curtailed, it would have turned a $70.6 Million curtailment cost to the grid, into a $91.5 Million Bitcoin mining revenue opportunity. Plus, by dealing with renewable intermittency at the front end of the queue, there could be even more renewable energy on the grid, which would have further reduced expenses by meaning fewer gas plants were called upon.

As we saw in the section on subsidies, this is not a fantasy: since 2021, Bitcoin mining companies helped catalyze an extra 50 GW of VRE generation on ERCOT’s grid alone.

Summary

As we can see, the areas where Bitcoin mining is solving major systemic issues with the grid are both wide and deep. Both peer reviewed research and actual real life case studies have showcased how Bitcoin is able to overcome the challenges of our current energy system which is centralized, subsidized, politicized, fossilized and wasteful.

These are the five reasons that the energy sector needs Bitcoin mining. There are also economic drivers that mean Bitcoin mining companies need to become energy companies. Together, these pull and push factors are the reasons that convergence of Bitcoin mining and energy are happening rapidly.

“The wise do not desire to do anything’ and the wise do not desire to abandon action either” ~ Yoga Vasistha

Here we tackle a topical question: what will happen to the world under two different scenarios: grids packed with Bitcoin mining vs grids packed with AI datacenters?

First some context: right now, Bitcoin mining and AI data centers are in a power struggle for power on the grid. Basically there’s not enough power and too many users wanting that power, especially in the US, where the grid has not increased its generation capacity since 2007: that’s 17 years!

So two tribes; limited resources. Sounds like a recipe for tension right? Let’s find out.

First let’s understand each tribe. The key difference between Bitcoin mining and AI/HPC data centers is in their energy consumption patterns. Bitcoin mining can ramp up or throttle down their energy usage on a dime. This flexibility makes them perfect for balancing out the fluctuating energy supply from renewables.

On the other hand, AI data centers need 24/7 uptime. This means they're not as adaptable to the ebbs and flows of renewable energy.

So while AI data centers are busy crunching numbers and trying to figure out why we humans are so weird, Bitcoin miners are out there, flexing their energy consumption muscles and helping to stabilize the grid.

As we can see though in this graphic below from a whitepaper by Rhodes et al, Flexible data centers like Bitcoin mining operations help grid operators to de-carbonize grids, whereas inflexible data centers mean grid operators must build more fossil-fuel baseload onto the grid to meet their 24/7 requirements.

The authors were independent energy experts from outside the Bitcoin ecosystem, and the paper they wrote is probably the most important paper ever written about Bitcoin and its impact on grids, because the repercussions are so huge.

Extrapolating Rhodes’ findings into the future, it’s no stretch to say that whether it’s more Bitcoin mining, or more AI on the grid could determine whether grids meet their net zero emission targets.

It’s a little known secret that Bitcoin data centers are the world’s most flexible data centers.

So next time you hear someone verbally copy&paste some journalist’s latest piece of Bitcoin gaslighting, ask them how they feel about AI data centers.

Any way you cut it, if your goal is net zero emissions, Bitcoin mining moves us closer to that target, whereas AI datacenters move us further away from it.
